arguments_rejected_or_waived: Petitioner's attempt to defend the Petition with new facts in her answering brief: rejected. Having chosen not to amend by the answering-brief deadline under Rule 15(a)(5), she cannot amend through her brief. Rule 15(d) supplementation would not reach events between July 2025 and the Petition date.

Petitioner's argument that Respondent's handling of her books-and-records demands should relax the pleading standards in her favor: rejected. She did not follow through on § 220, and filing a plenary action certifies she had enough information to plead.

Petitioner's argument (citing Mott v. State) that the same-claim and adverse-decision elements of res judicata were not met: rejected. It relied on matters outside the Petition, and the Uden/Cattlytx dual-role allegations were not pleaded as an independent or derivative claim.

Petitioner's argument that claims should be divided between this case and the Colorado Litigation if her Rule 60(b) motion succeeds: rejected. Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(c)(2) means the pending motion does not affect finality.

Petitioner's argument that she lacked a full and fair opportunity to litigate because her counsel abandoned the case: rejected. A Rule 41(b) penalty dismissal is an adjudication on the merits, and Hughes v. Trans World Airlines is distinguished. Her remedies were appeal or a malpractice claim against counsel.
Petitioner's argument that Savage v. Himes is distinguishable: rejected. Both cases involve a dismissal for failure to prosecute, and the remedy was appeal, not a collateral second suit.

Respondent's argument that the Petition was frivolous because Petitioner knew it was precluded: rejected. ASB Allegiance is distinguished, and without an evidentiary hearing there is no clear and convincing evidence she knew her allegations were false, given her asserted reliance on counsel's statements that the case remained 'still valid' and his encouragement to file here.

Respondent's argument that Petitioner acted in bad faith by characterizing the CEO shareholder letter as showing HerdDogg was 'structurally insolvent' and omitting that the Colorado Litigation caused the financial strain: rejected. Beck arose under Rule 37, the statement was not 'extremely probative,' the Court was not misled, and the conduct falls far short of Arbitrium.
Respondent's request for an anti-filing restriction on bad-faith and unclean-hands grounds: rejected. The record does not support a prophylactic filing restriction.
Respondent's reliance on 10 Del. C. § 5106 for attorneys' fees: rejected (fn. 276). § 5106 covers costs, not fees.

summary.brief_summary: Pro se founder-stockholder Melissa Brandao petitioned under 8 Del. C. § 291 for a receiver of HerdDogg, Inc., which moved to dismiss and for Rule 11 sanctions; Magistrate Fox issued a final report on both motions. The Court found the insolvency allegations stale and conclusory, and the governance allegations derivative but not pleaded under Rule 23.1. The Court held the Petition independently barred by res judicata, collateral estoppel and laches, because a Colorado federal court had dismissed her earlier suit, which also sought a receiver on the same facts, with prejudice for failure to prosecute, and she did not appeal. Sanctions were denied because Respondent did not show clear evidence of bad faith or knowing frivolousness, given Petitioner's asserted reliance on her former counsel.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether a founder-stockholder's 8 Del. C. § 291 petition for a receiver of HerdDogg, Inc. states a claim where insolvency rests on Q3 2024 financials, and whether it is barred by res judicata, collateral estoppel and laches after a federal court dismissed her earlier suit, which also sought a receiver on the same facts, with prejudice for failure to prosecute. A second issue is whether Respondent showed sanctionable conduct under Ct. Ch. R. 11 or the bad-faith exception to the American Rule.
summary.disposition: recommended: granted in part and denied in part
summary.holding: Final report recommending that the Motion to Dismiss be granted with prejudice and that the Motion for Sanctions be denied ('This is a final report... exceptions are governed by Rule 144'; exceptions due 11 days after entry because the matter was not expedited). (1) The Petition fails to state a § 291 claim. Insolvency rested on stale Q3 2024 data and conclusory assertions about unsalable assets and liabilities, and the Company's continued existence two years later undercuts alleged 'imminent exhaustion.' The insolvency 'plus' governance and dual-role allegations are speculative and derivative and not pleaded under Rule 23.1. (2) The Petition is barred by res judicata and collateral estoppel because the Colorado Litigation's final, unappealed penalty dismissal with prejudice adjudicated on the merits the same parties, the same receiver request and the same nucleus of facts, and the pending Rule 60(b) motion does not affect finality. (3) On these 'unusual conditions,' laches bars the Petition: Petitioner knew the facts, did not appeal, waited five months to refile in a new forum, and Respondent is prejudiced by defending the same claims again. The dismissal bars any further filing that relies on HerdDogg's Q3 2024 financials or earlier financial status and transactions as a basis for insolvency. Sanctions were denied. Respondent did not show by clear evidence that Petitioner lacked an objective good-faith belief, given her asserted reliance on Mr. Oleske's statements and his encouragement to file here. The shareholder-letter characterization was 'at most a purposeful mischaracterization' that did not mislead the Court. No anti-filing restriction was imposed. The Court decided the motions on the papers without an evidentiary hearing, left any consequences for Mr. Oleske to the disciplinary authorities, and urged Petitioner to retain counsel for any future litigation.
key_facts_and_concessions: The Petition's insolvency allegations rested on Q3 2024 financial information and the absence of later disclosures. Petitioner conceded in her answering brief that Respondent's description of that data as stale 'was accurate as to the four corners of the Petition.'

Petitioner's earlier suit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado (RICO, COCCA, patent and state-law claims against HerdDogg and others) sought appointment of a permanent receiver on the same alleged insolvency, insider self-dealing, forged patent assignments and investor misrepresentations.

The Colorado court dismissed the Colorado Litigation with prejudice on January 23, 2026 'as a sanction for Plaintiff's noncompliance' after Petitioner did not respond to four motions or to an order to show cause. Time to appeal elapsed February 23, 2026, and a Rule 60(b) motion filed August 5, 2026 remains pending.

Petitioner filed the Petition on June 23, 2026, five months after the dismissal. Her filings here did not mention the Colorado Litigation until Respondent's answering brief on the motion to expedite raised it.
Petitioner chose to defend the Petition rather than amend under Rule 15(a)(5), and sought to add facts outside the Petition in her answering brief.
The Petition's prayer for relief sought only a receiver and related directives. It pleaded no Rule 23.1 demand or demand-futility allegations and did not identify the board.

At oral argument Petitioner conceded the Petition was drafted by Mr. Oleske, her former Colorado counsel, who withdrew on July 23/29, 2026. The Court received no independent evidence of the extent of his involvement. Fn. 266 notes Petitioner did learn from Respondent that the case was dismissed 'with prejudice,' but it is unclear what effect she understood that to have.
Respondent contested the Petition's facts but assumed them true solely for the Motion to Dismiss (fn. 214), so the motion was not converted to summary judgment.
summary.practical_takeaway: A litigant whose prior suit is dismissed with prejudice for failure to prosecute must pursue an appeal (or a malpractice claim) rather than refile the same claims in Chancery. On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, new or updated facts must come in by amendment before the answering-brief deadline, not through the brief. Sanction movants should expressly invoke the bad-faith exception and marshal clear evidence; reliance-on-counsel narratives can defeat a Rule 11 or fee-shifting request.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 12(b)(6) reasonable conceivability, with conclusory allegations not accepted. A § 291 receiver requires insolvency at filing by clear and convincing proof, a benefit or avoided harm from appointment, and benefits outweighing harms. Preclusion and laches were decided on the pleadings plus judicially noticed filings from the Colorado Litigation, applying Delaware preclusion standards out of caution. Rule 11 sanctions are judged by an objective standard and reserved for outrageous and abusive conduct; equitable fee shifting requires 'clear evidence' of bad faith.

entries.name: Invictus Special Situations Master I, L.P. v. Invictus Global Management, LLC, et al.,

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Delano, Patel and Invictus GP's argument that the Books and Records Order must be limited to IGM because only IGM was party to the Management Agreement: rejected. The argument was not raised at trial and was waived, it is subject to exceptions to the signatory rule, Defendants' own proposed order used the same language, and no clear error was shown given the control stipulation.

Delano's argument that the non-signatory point is "not a procedural technicality subject to waiver—it is a substantive limitation on liability": rejected as incorrect, because the argument can be waived (fn. 51, citing Medicalgorithmics).
Defendants' request to amend the Retained Funds Order: rejected. The form was negotiated and agreed to without objection, and the order mentions only IGM.

Delano's reliance on Frederick-Conaway v. Baird for clarifying "sloppy" language: distinguished. Here the two judgments are not clearly in error and use language similar, if not identical, to language the parties submitted or agreed to.

Delano's supplemental argument that the Supreme Court's corrected opinion is a new and material addition to the law of the case that forecloses any fiduciary-duty basis for reaching non-signatories: rejected as meritless. The Supreme Court said little about the earlier judgments, nothing suggests it meant to upend non-advancement rulings, and the Fund's claims were always grounded in the Management Agreement. The Court addressed it on the merits for completeness because the Fund had a chance to respond (fn. 61).

Patel, IGM and Invictus GP's Motion for Leave to vacate the Retained Funds Order and reopen discovery because delayed advancement prevented them from presenting evidence and expert testimony: rejected. The remedy is unheard of and, even if available, inappropriate given years of litigation with sophisticated Delaware counsel, largely self-inflicted delay, and no stay request or Rule 56(d) affidavit.

Movants' contention that new evidence and an expert affidavit would have tipped the scales: merits not reached, but fn. 68 notes, as the Fund points out, that the "new" evidence was in the summary judgment record. It also notes that the relevance of expert testimony on debtor-in-possession lending market practice to IGM's post-termination withholding is unclear.

summary.brief_summary: In the Fund's expedited suit against its removed manager IGM, its former general partner Invictus GP and principals Patel and Delano, Vice Chancellor Cook, in a letter decision, denied Defendants' Rule 54(b) motion to amend the Books and Records Order and Retained Funds Order. The Court also denied a motion by Patel, IGM and Invictus GP to supplement that motion and vacate the Retained Funds Order on the ground that advancement was delayed until the Supreme Court's April 2026 ruling. Applying the law of the case, the Court held that the argument that only IGM, as sole signatory to the Management Agreement, could be bound was waived because it was not raised at trial and contradicted Defendants' own proposed order, and that the Retained Funds Order was agreed to and names only IGM. Delano's reliance on the Supreme Court's corrected opinion was rejected as meritless, and the do-over request failed given Defendants' self-inflicted delay and their failure to seek a stay or Rule 56(d) relief.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether, under Ct. Ch. R. 54(b) and the law-of-the-case doctrine, the Court should revise (i) the Books and Records Order and Retained Funds Order to run only against IGM, the sole signatory to the Management Agreement, on a non-signatory argument first raised after those orders were entered, and (ii) vacate the Retained Funds Order and reopen discovery because IGM did not receive advancement until after the Supreme Court's April 2026 ruling.
summary.holding: Both the Motion to Amend and the Motion for Leave are denied, and Delano's supplemental submissions are rejected on the merits. The Court held that the Motion to Amend identified no clear error, injustice or changed circumstances that would overcome the law of the case. The non-signatory argument could have been raised in early 2024 and was waived; Defendants' own proposed order used the challenged "Defendants" language; and the agreed Retained Funds Order names only IGM. Allowing the argument now would reward a strategic decision to hold back arguments in bifurcated proceedings and then claim legal error under Rule 54(b). The Supreme Court's corrected wording did not change the law of the case on the non-advancement rulings, because the Fund's claims were always grounded in the Management Agreement. On the Motion for Leave, the Court called the requested vacatur and reopened discovery "extraordinary" and unheard of. It declined to decide how a remedy for delayed advancement interacts with the law of the case, holding instead that the remedy would be inappropriate even if available: Defendants had sophisticated counsel, caused much of the delay themselves, and never sought a stay or filed a Rule 56(d) affidavit. The Court expressed hope that the ruling closes the book on the merits of each side's claims and counterclaims at the trial court level, and asked the parties to bring the rest of the proceeding to an orderly close.
key_facts_and_concessions: Defendants did not raise the non-signatory argument at the February 2024 Books and Records trial. Their own proposed order, filed with their post-trial brief, would have compelled "Defendants . . . to turn over to the Fund" documents "in the possession and control of Invictus Global Management, LLC," the language they now attack.
The Retained Funds Order was a form of order "agreed-to" by the parties, and nobody objected at the time. Its operative clauses mention only IGM.
The parties stipulated that Patel and Delano "controlled IGM at all relevant times" (fn. 53).
The Management Agreement was signed only by IGM, and the parties always knew Patel and Delano did not sign it individually (fn. 58).

Much of the delay was self-inflicted. Defendants removed the case to federal court on a Saturday five days before the January 2024 trial, counsel did not appear at the pre-trial conference two days later, and the District Court remanded, finding the removal untimely and meritless. Defendants' discovery positions had already narrowed that trial.

During summary judgment briefing on the Retained Funds issue, Defendants did not request a stay, submit a Rule 56(d) affidavit, or otherwise suggest they could not mount a defense without the evidence they now say was necessary.

The Supreme Court's interlocutory appeal resolved advancement in Defendants' favor (ERISA § 1110 no bar) but did not include either order in its scope (fn. 34). Its corrected opinion changed "state-law fiduciary duty claims in state court" to "state-law claims in state court."

Patel, IGM and Invictus GP conceded they were "unaware of any decision by this Court related to amending a judgment as an equitable remedy to correct the injustices that results from a wrongful failure to advance fees and expenses."
summary.practical_takeaway: Raise any objection to which defendants an implementing order binds, including non-signatory defenses, during the relevant bifurcated phase and before the form of order is entered, and do not propose or agree to order language you may later attack. A party claiming that unpaid advancement leaves it unable to defend on summary judgment should seek a stay or file a Rule 56(d) affidavit at the time rather than ask later for vacatur.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 54(b) revision of interlocutory orders, governed at a minimum by the law-of-the-case standard: a ruling will not be disturbed absent a compelling reason, such as clear error, a sufficient equitable concern of preventing injustice, or an important change of circumstances.

entries.name: In re WideOpenWest, Inc. Stockholders' Litigation

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Turk Faction's argument that LBP's 43% sell-down between signing and closing undercuts its leadership claim: rejected. LBP's explanation that the sales were portfolio rebalancing makes sense for an institution, the sales are unlikely to matter, and Turk conceded he also sold, which "takes the wind out of this argument's sails."

Turk Faction's argument that appointing LBP risks exposing the class to a fair price defense: rejected. Counsel could not identify a case in which a representative plaintiff's pre-litigation views on value, based on public information, were material to a fair price determination. If they mattered, the class's valuation case would already be in trouble.

Turk Faction's argument that Turk's pre-closing repurchases make him less of a net seller and show his commitment to the suit: does not compel a different outcome. Fn. 47 notes this may itself create defense arguments.

Turk Faction's argument that Turk should have pole position because his stake was a larger share of his portfolio: rejected. The economic-stakes factor is a "wash," although LBP could be deemed to have the edge from its massive stake.

Turk Faction's argument that the LBP Faction is an unwieldy "committee of the willing" of six firms: rejected. LBP proposed a two-firm leadership structure led by excellent counsel, and the Turk Faction did not press the point at oral argument.

Turk Faction's argument that its counsel's discovery work in the related appraisal actions should count and that LBP pursued overlapping discovery: rejected as neutral, because neither faction had access to the appraisal discovery.

Each faction's argument that its pleading was superior: rejected as neutral. Both relied on Section 220 materials, neither faces significant dispositive-motion risk, and defendants have already answered.

Both factions used books-and-records demands to draft their complaints.

summary.brief_summary: In a consolidated stockholder class action challenging the take-private Merger of WideOpenWest, Inc. by controller Crestview Advisors, L.L.C. and DigitalBridge Investments, LLC, two factions cross-moved for appointment as lead plaintiff and lead counsel: the LBP Faction (LB Partners LLC and ODS Capital LLC) and the Turk Faction (individual investor Matthew Turk). Vice Chancellor Cook found every contested Rule 23(d)(4)(A) factor neutral, including relative economic stakes, where both stakes were substantial. The Court broke the tie on additional characteristics, favoring LBP as a sophisticated institutional manager of endowment and family capital over an individual whose background was not disclosed until the Court asked. The Court rejected the Turk Faction's attacks based on LBP's signing-to-closing sales, noting Turk had sold too.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether, in a consolidated class action challenging the take-private Merger of WideOpenWest, Inc. by its controller Crestview and DigitalBridge, the LBP Faction or the Turk Faction should be appointed lead plaintiff and lead counsel under Ct. Ch. R. 23(d)(4)(A), where the Hirt factors are neutral and the tiebreaker is the proposed lead plaintiffs' additional characteristics.
summary.holding: The LBP Faction's motion was granted and the Turk Faction's competing motion denied. LBP and ODS were appointed lead plaintiffs, Bernstein Litowitz Berger & Grossmann LLP and Block & Leviton LLP co-lead counsel, and Labaton Keller Sucharow LLP and Friedman & Tejtel PLLC additional counsel. The contested Hirt factors were all neutral: pleading quality, performance to date, and leadership structure. Both stakes were substantial on an absolute and relative basis, so the economic-stakes factor was a wash. The Court said LBP could be deemed to have the edge, but deciding between excellent teams "is an art and not a science." As the tiebreaker under Fox, LBP's institutional sophistication, its experience managing third-party capital, and its "enormous stake" made it the clear choice, especially because Turk never explained who he was until the Court asked at the hearing. LBP's signing-to-closing sales did not change the result. They were a sensible rebalancing, unlikely to matter to fair price, and offset by Turk's own sales, which were disclosed late. In fn. 44 the Court added that a lead plaintiff whose valuation is "tethered to the real world" may not be a negative.
key_facts_and_concessions: Turk filed no affidavit on his WOW holdings or background before the hearing, and his briefing did not say who he was. The Court had to ask at the hearing, where counsel said Turk is an individual investing for himself and his wife.

LBP held 3,888,326 shares ($20.2 million in Merger consideration). It was WOW's largest unaffiliated stockholder (about 7% of the unaffiliated float), and WOW was about 17% of the securities LBP reported on Form 13F.
Turk held 900,000 shares ($4.5 million), about 20% of his portfolio and, according to LBP, under 2% of the public float.
The Turk Faction conceded that "LBP also has a sufficient stake to incentiv[ize] it to monitor."

LBP is a sophisticated fund founded by Charles Pollard Cocke, Jr., a former UVA Investment Management Company analyst who spent 16 years building Investure LLC into a manager of about $14 billion for nonprofit endowments and foundations. LBP is also his family's de facto investment office, and the family is the largest investor across LBP's funds.

LBP sold 43% of its WOW stake between signing and closing. Turk also sold between signing and closing for liquidity, which was disclosed only in a docket letter filed the day before the hearing; he later bought back shares shortly before closing (fn. 47-48).
Both factions ran 8 Del. C. § 220 investigations. Defendants answered the LBP complaint and offered to stipulate that the answer would also serve as their answer to the Turk complaint.
Neither faction had access to the written discovery in the related appraisal actions; the Turk Faction said it knew "very little" about that discovery.
summary.practical_takeaway: Proposed lead plaintiffs should put their identity, holdings, and fiduciary or investment experience before the Court by affidavit in the opening leadership papers, because positive characteristics can decide a contest when the Hirt factors are even. Before attacking a rival's trading, check and disclose your own client's trading: a late-revealed matching sale can neutralize the argument and damage credibility.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 23(d)(4)(A) (codified Hirt factors); a "nuanced and case-specific" analysis aimed at a leadership structure that will provide effective representation, with relative economic stakes given "great weight."
